steps.caption: Scripted keyboard navigation demo (automated). Not a screen reader demonstration: VoiceOver automation is unavailable on macOS 27, so no spoken output is shown. Captions describe the scripted keyboard steps.
The module home page loads. Every page starts with a skip link as the first tab stop.
Tab once — the skip link receives a visible focus outline.
Enter activates the skip link; focus jumps past the navigation to the main content.
Tab moves through the module navigation links.
Enter opens the Lesson page.
The lesson page: the study outline as semantic HTML with headings, lists, and a data table with a caption and scoped headers.
Tab reaches the Schools of Psychological Thought table; row and column headers are announced to assistive technology via scope attributes.
Arrow keys move between row headers in the table.
Next: the lecture slides page, where the 54-slide deck is HTML with real text, figure descriptions, and speaker notes.
Tab through the page; a details element expands the long description of a visual.
Enter expands the long description of the slide’s visual.
The expanded long description is visible to sighted users and read by screen readers alike.
The video page: a standard video element with a captions track, chapter buttons, and a transcript link.
Tab to a chapter button.
Enter starts playback from that chapter — the video element is fully keyboard operable.
The player controls are native and keyboard accessible; captions load from the transcript-derived WebVTT file.
Last: the practice quiz.
Tab to the first question’s radio group.
Arrow keys move within the radio group — radios use arrow-key navigation.
Space selects an answer.
Tab to the Check answer button.
Enter checks the answer; feedback appears in a live region that assistive technology announces.
Textual feedback is shown — never color alone. The score region updates politely.

Every check shown here is scripted; see the case study’s evidence section for the full audit, and the limitations section for what remains pending — including a human VoiceOver pass and a review by a daily assistive-technology user.
